title: Academic English examples
scope: Original teaching examples from everyday and research contexts. These are practice illustrations, not empirical findings.

plural.subject: Community gardening
plural.task: Complete: The pots beside the greenhouse ___ daily watering. (need / needs)
plural.answer: need → The pots beside the greenhouse need daily watering.
moves: Find the subject head: pots.
Pots is plural. The nearby singular noun greenhouse does not control the verb.
plural.transfer: Find the head of your subject, then enter only the missing verb.
plural.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

singular.subject: Museum visits
singular.task: Complete: The cost of the guided tours ___ on their length. (depend / depends)
singular.answer: depends → The cost of the guided tours depends on their length.
moves: The head is cost, not tours.
Singular cost takes depends.
singular.transfer: Ignore intervening phrases when checking agreement.
singular.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

articles.subject: Birdwatching
articles.task: Complete: We saw ___ owl. Later, ___ owl returned. (a / an / the)
articles.answer: an / the → We saw an owl. Later, the owl returned.
moves: An introduces one countable bird before a vowel sound.
The refers back to that identified bird.
articles.transfer: Check sound and whether the reader can identify the referent. Enter multiple gaps with /.
articles.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

preposition.subject: Baking
preposition.task: Complete: The texture depends ___ the amount of water.
preposition.answer: on → The texture depends on the amount of water.
moves: Learn depends on as a word and its complement.
The preposition expresses the dependency; it is not chosen from a general rule about all verbs.
preposition.transfer: Identify the word or expression that governs the gap.
preposition.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

contrast.subject: A school library
contrast.task: Choose although or despite: ___ the library has many books, students cannot borrow them after 4 p.m.
contrast.answer: Although the library has many books, students cannot borrow them after 4 p.m.
moves: The first idea creates an expectation of access.
The second limits that expectation.
Although is followed by a subject and verb: the library has.
contrast.transfer: Connect a real concession, then check the grammatical form after the connector.
contrast.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

despite.subject: A school library
despite.task: Complete with a noun phrase: Despite ___, students cannot borrow books after 4 p.m.
despite.answer: Despite its large collection, students cannot borrow books after 4 p.m.
moves: Its large collection is a noun phrase.
The main clause states the limit on access.
despite.transfer: Use a noun phrase or -ing form after despite; do not write despite + a bare finite clause.
despite.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

conditions.subject: A museum workshop
conditions.task: Meaning: a booking is necessary, but the workshop might still be cancelled. Complete: Visitors can attend only ___ they have a booking.
conditions.answer: if → Visitors can attend only if they have a booking.
moves: Only if marks a necessary condition.
A booking alone does not guarantee that the workshop takes place.
conditions.transfer: Check the direction of the condition, not just whether the sentence sounds grammatical.
conditions.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

because.subject: Gardening
because.task: Choose because or therefore: The gardener moved the seedlings indoors ___ frost was forecast.
because.answer: because → The gardener moved the seedlings indoors because frost was forecast.
moves: The second clause supplies the reason for the action.
A consequence could instead follow a semicolon: Frost was forecast; therefore, the gardener moved the seedlings indoors.
because.transfer: Identify reason and consequence before choosing the connector. A connector cannot supply an absent premise.
because.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

affect.subject: Baking
affect.task: Complete: Oven temperature can ___ the crust. We measured its ___. (affect / effect)
affect.answer: affect / effect → Oven temperature can affect the crust. We measured its effect.
moves: After can, affect is a verb meaning influence.
After its, effect is a noun naming a result.
affect.transfer: Use the grammatical position as well as the intended meaning.
affect.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

countable.subject: A museum
countable.task: Complete: We sold ___ tickets and have ___ time to prepare. (fewer / less)
countable.answer: fewer / less → We sold fewer tickets and have less time to prepare.
moves: Tickets are counted as individual objects.
Time is treated as an uncountable quantity here.
countable.transfer: Check the noun in this context, not the size of the quantity.
countable.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

parallel.subject: A cooking class
parallel.task: Complete: Students can weigh the flour, mix the dough and ___ the loaves. (shape / shaping / shaped)
parallel.answer: shape → Students can weigh the flour, mix the dough and shape the loaves.
moves: Weigh, mix and shape are parallel base-form verbs after can.
All three operations belong to the same list.
parallel.transfer: Keep coordinated operations in the same grammatical form.
parallel.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

auxiliary.subject: A bus timetable
auxiliary.task: Complete: The revised timetable does not ___ every connection. (guarantee / guarantees)
auxiliary.answer: guarantee → The revised timetable does not guarantee every connection.
moves: Does carries tense and agreement.
The verb after does not stays in its base form.
auxiliary.transfer: Look for the auxiliary before choosing the following verb form.
auxiliary.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

word-choice.subject: A museum survey
word-choice.task: Choose a precise word: The survey ___ that visitors preferred morning tours. (suggests / proves)
word-choice.answer: The survey suggests that visitors preferred morning tours.
moves: The report concerns the people surveyed.
Proves would need much stronger justification and a clearly stated proposition.
word-choice.transfer: Choose words that fit the evidence; a more emphatic word is not more academic.
word-choice.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

reference.subject: A library
reference.task: Replace the vague reference: The catalogue lists opening hours. This helps with this.
reference.answer: The catalogue lists opening hours. This information helps visitors plan when to arrive.
moves: This information points to the listed hours.
The second clause names the concrete purpose rather than repeating this.
reference.transfer: Name what your reference refers to and what connection the reader should make.
reference.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

demonstrative.subject: Gardening
demonstrative.task: Complete: ___ three seedlings need larger pots. (This / These)
demonstrative.answer: These three seedlings need larger pots.
moves: Seedlings is plural.
These refers to more than one item.
demonstrative.transfer: Match this/that or these/those to the number of the noun.
demonstrative.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

uncountable.subject: Local history
uncountable.task: Complete: The archive provides useful ___. (evidence / evidences)
moves: Evidence is normally uncountable in this use.
To count distinct items, write three pieces of evidence and identify them.
uncountable.transfer: Use the uncountable form in the gap; distinguish evidence from the documents that supply it.
uncountable.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

units.subject: A library survey
units.task: Thirty of 50 surveyed visitors arrived by bus. Choose the correct claim: 60% of surveyed visitors / 60% of all local residents.
units.answer: 60% of surveyed visitors arrived by bus.
moves: The numerator is 30 visitors who arrived by bus.
The denominator is the 50 people surveyed, not the town population.
units.transfer: Keep the population, unit and denominator attached to your number.
units.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

levels.subject: School attendance
levels.task: Explain the distinction: attendance is recorded for individual pupils; summaries are reported for classes.
levels.answer: Attendance is recorded at the pupil level and summarised across classes. A class average does not show whether a particular pupil was absent.
moves: The first sentence separates the unit of observation from the reporting group.
The second explains what cannot be inferred for an individual.
levels.transfer: Name each unit explicitly and check which direction of inference your own task allows.
levels.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

job.subject: Community gardening
job.task: A paragraph says volunteers can water only six beds per morning and explains why beds must be inspected in an order. Choose its job: motivate a priority / report a harvest / define a tool.
moves: The paragraph explains why a decision is necessary.
It does not yet report the success of any treatment.
job.transfer: Choose the purpose of this paragraph, not the general subject of the whole paper.
job.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

order.subject: A community garden
order.task: Order the moves: A: prioritise inspection; B: limited time; C: inspect soil before choosing treatment; D: cannot inspect every bed today.
order.answer:
B D A C
Volunteers have limited time. They cannot inspect every bed today, so they need to prioritise inspection. Soil checks are still needed before choosing a treatment.
moves: B supplies the constraint.
D explains its practical consequence.
A states the resulting decision.
C keeps inspection priority separate from treatment choice.
order.transfer: Use every supplied part once. Type letters with spaces or click the parts; special arrows are unnecessary.
order.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

definition.subject: A lending library
definition.task: Define a reservation and state its boundary in two sentences.
definition.answer: A reservation is a request to hold a book for a named reader when a copy becomes available. It does not mean that the reader has already borrowed the book.
moves: The first sentence names the category and the defining condition.
The second distinguishes a related action that the term does not mean.
definition.transfer: Write what your concept means in this context. Keep its defining features separate from hoped-for benefits.
definition.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

subject.subject: A museum
subject.task: Make the actor clear: A checking of tickets is carried out before entry.
subject.answer: A steward checks each ticket before the visitor enters.
moves: A steward answers who performs the action.
Checks replaces the abstract phrase a checking is carried out.
Passive voice would also work if the actor were unknown or unimportant.
subject.transfer: Identify what acts, changes or is measured. Use active or passive voice according to what the reader needs.
subject.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

bridge.subject: A community garden
bridge.task: Idea A: Volunteers can inspect only six beds today. Idea B: They need an order for inspecting the beds. Supply the missing reason in one or two sentences.
bridge.answer: Because some beds will remain uninspected today, inspecting them in an arbitrary order could leave the driest beds unchecked. An order based on signs of dryness would make those beds the first candidates for inspection.
moves: A gives a capacity limit.
The missing premise is that postponing inspection matters more for some beds than for others; dryness is the stated hypothetical criterion.
B is justified by that difference. The example does not establish which treatment will help.
Merely writing “Time is limited; therefore, an order is needed” leaves the criterion and consequence unexplained.
bridge.transfer: Choose two ideas in your task. Explain why the first supports or qualifies the second. State an assumption if that connection has not yet been established. Write the linking explanation, not a whole paragraph.
bridge.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

evidence.subject: A library
evidence.task: Sort two claims: 18 of 30 surveyed visitors requested later opening; later opening will improve exam results. State the support and the gap.
evidence.answer:
Claim | Support | Still unknown
Visitors requested later opening | 18 responses in this survey | Whether other visitors share that preference
Later opening improves exam results | No exam-outcome evidence supplied | Whether changing the hours affects results
The survey supports a claim about reported preferences, not an effect on exam results.
moves: The first row links a bounded claim to actual supplied evidence.
The second marks an unsupported causal claim as a gap.
The final sentence explains the different evidential status.
evidence.transfer: Name the evidence needed; do not invent a citation or treat a citation key as verified support.
evidence.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

qualification.subject: A bus route
qualification.task: Write a result with a useful limitation: 8 of 10 observed buses arrived on time on Tuesday morning.
qualification.answer: Eight of the ten buses observed on Tuesday morning arrived on time. This observation does not establish the route’s reliability on other days.
moves: The result retains its numerator, denominator and observation window.
The limitation identifies exactly where the evidence stops.
qualification.transfer: State a relevant boundary; adding may to an unsupported claim does not supply evidence.
qualification.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

handover.subject: A library
handover.task: Paragraph 1 establishes a need for evening access. Paragraph 2 will assess possible opening hours. Write their handover.
handover.answer: Demand for evening access leaves a practical question: which additional hours can the library staff cover? The next paragraph compares two schedules against the available staffing hours.
moves: The end of paragraph 1 names a question left unresolved.
The start of paragraph 2 picks up that question and states its distinct job.
handover.transfer: Identify what your current paragraph leaves open and what the next one will actually answer. A heading alone does not supply the reasoning.
handover.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

paragraph.subject: A community garden
paragraph.task: Use these ideas in a short paragraph: six beds can be inspected today; dryness varies; inspection comes before a treatment decision. This is a compact structural model, not a target word count.
paragraph.answer: The volunteers need a basis for deciding which beds to inspect first. They can inspect only six beds today, and signs of dryness vary across the garden. If the aim is to avoid overlooking beds that may need water, those signs provide a provisional basis for ordering inspections. The order identifies where to look first; soil checks are still needed before deciding whether to water a particular bed.
moves: Job: motivate a decision.
Support: limited capacity and a relevant difference between beds.
Reason: postponement may matter differently under the stated aim.
Boundary: inspection is distinct from treatment.
paragraph.transfer: Keep the reasoning roles, close this example, and draft from your own checked ideas. Follow the length requested in your task; you need not use one sentence per role.
paragraph.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

transfer.subject: A museum
transfer.task: Transfer the idea of evidence plus boundary to this new situation: 12 of 20 surveyed visitors liked a longer tour; no new tour has been tested.
transfer.answer: Twelve of the twenty visitors surveyed preferred a longer tour. Their responses support testing demand for that option, but they do not establish whether visitors would enjoy an actual longer tour. A trial could examine that question. The transferred writing principle is to separate a reported preference from an observed effect.
moves: Only the new situation’s facts are used.
The boundary explains why a test is needed.
The last sentence names the writing principle, not a research-domain concept.
transfer.transfer: Transfer the reasoning pattern. Do not carry over numbers, technical terms or conclusions from the old situation.
transfer.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

observation.subject: Gardening
observation.task: Of ten shaded pots and ten sunny pots, six shaded pots and two sunny pots wilted. No other conditions were controlled. Report an observation, then a possible explanation.
observation.answer: Wilting occurred in six shaded pots and two sunny pots. Differences in watering might explain the pattern, but watering was not controlled or measured in this comparison.
moves: The first sentence reports counts.
The second labels a possible explanation and identifies missing evidence.
The observed association does not isolate a cause.
observation.transfer: Keep observation, interpretation and causal evidence distinct.
observation.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

two-contrasts.subject: A library
two-contrasts.task: Express this concession in two forms: the collection is large, but evening access is restricted.
two-contrasts.answer:
Although the library has a large collection, evening access is restricted.
Despite its large collection, the library offers restricted evening access.
moves: Although is followed by a clause.
Despite is followed by a noun phrase.
The same contrast is retained in both sentences; although does not need an extra but.
two-contrasts.transfer: Write two sentences with equivalent meaning, changing the grammar after the connector.
two-contrasts.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

method.subject: Baking
method.task: Describe three operations: weigh flour; add water; record kneading time. Identify one missing detail needed for repetition.
method.answer: The baker first weighs the flour. She then adds water and records the kneading time. To repeat the procedure, another baker would also need the flour-to-water ratio, which this brief does not specify.
moves: The stated sequence is retained.
The actor and operations are explicit.
A missing reproducibility detail is identified without inventing its value.
method.transfer: Use the operations supplied in your task. Name settings that still need to be specified.
method.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

comparison.subject: A museum
comparison.task: Compare a 30-minute and a 60-minute tour in three sentences; visitor ratings and staffing costs are not yet available.
comparison.answer: The museum could compare the two tour lengths using the same exhibits and visitor recruitment procedure. Visitor ratings would address experience, while staff hours would show the resource demand. Both measurements are still needed before choosing a schedule.
moves: The options share a stated comparison basis.
Different criteria are named separately.
The example does not announce an unmeasured winner.
comparison.transfer: Name the alternatives, the common basis and the evidence still needed.
comparison.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

two-method.subject: A library
two-method.task: Explain two operations: record a visitor’s preferred opening hour; count responses for each hour.
two-method.answer: The librarian records each respondent’s preferred opening hour. She then counts the responses for each hour to describe the preferences in this survey.
moves: One sentence explains collection at the response level.
The next explains aggregation and its limited purpose.
two-method.transfer: Explain what each operation does and how the second uses the first. Avoid adding an untested benefit.
two-method.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

advanced-argument.subject: A library
advanced-argument.task: Build a bounded argument from 18 requests for evening access among 30 survey responses; no extended hours were tested.
advanced-argument.answer: The library has a reason to investigate evening opening, but the survey does not yet justify a permanent schedule change. Eighteen of the thirty respondents requested later access. That pattern establishes interest within this group and gives the proposed change a concrete question to address: whether demand would turn into actual use. Respondents may differ from visitors who did not take part, and a stated preference is not attendance. A limited trial, with attendance recorded by hour, would help assess use before the library commits staff time to a new schedule.
moves: Claim: investigate, rather than announce a proven benefit.
Evidence: a bounded survey count.
Reason: demand provides a question for testing.
Limit and next step: preference and use require different evidence.
advanced-argument.transfer: Develop the claim–evidence connection and the reason for the next step; follow your task’s word range.
advanced-argument.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

alternatives.subject: Gardening
alternatives.task: Some seedlings have yellow leaves. Watering records and soil measurements are unavailable. Compare two explanations without deciding prematurely.
alternatives.answer: Yellow leaves alone do not distinguish excess watering from a nutrient shortage. Both are candidate explanations in this hypothetical example, but the brief supplies no measurements that favour either one. Watering records and an inspection of drainage could help examine the first account. A soil assessment could address the second. Neither check should be described as a completed diagnosis, and other explanations may remain possible. The useful conclusion is therefore about what to investigate: the observations identify a problem, while the proposed checks address why it might have occurred.
moves: Both explanations are represented as candidates.
Different evidence is linked to each.
The conclusion preserves the unresolved choice.
alternatives.transfer: State what would distinguish your alternatives instead of selecting the explanation that sounds most fluent.
alternatives.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

synthesis.subject: Museum learning
synthesis.task: Invented summaries: Study A counts visits to exhibits but does not measure recall. Study B measures recall after a guided visit but does not compare exhibit choices. Synthesise their contributions.
synthesis.answer: The two teaching studies address different parts of museum learning. Study A shows which exhibits visitors choose, whereas Study B examines what participants recall after a guided visit. Read together, they separate exposure to an exhibit from learning about its content. The visit counts cannot establish recall, and the recall test cannot explain visitors’ independent choices because the route was guided. A study that records exhibit choices and later tests recall in the same visitors could connect these questions. The existing summaries offer complementary measurements; they do not establish that the most frequently visited exhibit produces the most learning.
moves: The organising question is shared, not one summary per paragraph.
Each study contributes something distinct.
The gap follows from what neither study links.
synthesis.transfer: Use only the supplied study summaries. Keep invented teaching studies distinct from real citations.
synthesis.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

choice.subject: A library
choice.task: Choose provisionally between one extra evening or two extra mornings under an explicitly hypothetical staffing limit.
choice.answer: Suppose the library can fund four additional staff hours each week. Under that hypothetical limit, one extra evening would be a reasonable option to test if the aim is to serve visitors who cannot come during working hours. Two extra mornings would distribute access across more days, but they would not directly address that stated aim. The choice remains provisional because the brief gives no attendance estimates or staffing-cost differences. I would reconsider the evening option if a trial showed little evening use or if the required staff coverage exceeded the available hours.
moves: The constraint is labelled hypothetical.
The aim explains the trade-off.
A concrete reconsideration condition keeps the choice provisional.
choice.transfer: Separate assumptions you add for the exercise from supplied facts.
choice.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

counterargument.subject: A museum
counterargument.task: Respond fairly: “Longer tours always teach visitors more.” No comparative learning test is supplied.
counterargument.answer: A longer tour can provide time to discuss more exhibits, which is a reasonable motivation for extending it. More time alone, however, does not show that visitors learn more. The outcome could depend on the content, presentation and visitors’ attention, none of which is compared in this brief. The claim therefore moves from an opportunity for learning to an unmeasured learning outcome. A more defensible conclusion is that a longer tour is an option worth testing. A comparison using a defined recall measure would help establish whether the additional time improves learning in the setting studied.
moves: Acknowledge the plausible premise.
Locate the unsupported step.
Offer a bounded conclusion and a relevant test.
counterargument.transfer: Engage with the strongest reasonable version of the objection; do not dismiss it with a connector alone.
counterargument.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

future.subject: A bus survey
future.task: Separate uncertainty, consequence for the claim, and further work. Only Tuesday-morning arrivals have been observed.
future.answer:
The observation describes Tuesday-morning arrivals, but it is uncertain whether that pattern holds at other times. The brief contains no observations of evening journeys or weekend services.

This limited coverage prevents a claim about the route’s reliability throughout the week. It does not make the Tuesday observations useless: they still describe the journeys that were actually observed.

Further observations should cover the time periods to which a wider claim would apply. Recording both the number of journeys observed and the arrival criterion would allow the later comparison to use an explicit basis. That work is proposed, not already completed.
moves: Paragraph 1 names the missing knowledge.
Paragraph 2 explains which conclusion it prevents.
Paragraph 3 proposes work that addresses that specific gap.
future.transfer: Give each paragraph a distinct job. Avoid an unrelated list of future topics.
future.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

progression.subject: A museum
progression.task: Write two connected paragraphs: contribution of a visitor survey, then its boundary and a next step.
progression.answer:
A survey can help a museum identify questions about its tours. In this constructed example, twelve of twenty respondents requested more time at the paintings. That preference identifies one feature worth examining in a revised tour. It gives the museum a specific proposal to test, rather than a general instruction to improve the visitor experience.

Whether visitors would benefit from that change remains open. A request for more time is not a measurement of learning or enjoyment during a longer visit. A trial could therefore compare visitors’ experience under two stated schedules. The survey motivates the trial; it does not supply its outcome.
moves: Paragraph 1 establishes what the current evidence contributes.
The opening of paragraph 2 picks up the unresolved benefit.
Paragraph 2 develops a new job instead of summarising paragraph 1 again.
progression.transfer: Use the boundary of the first paragraph to motivate the second.
progression.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

reviewer.subject: A library
reviewer.task: A reviewer cannot distinguish survey evidence from an assumed benefit. Provide a response and a revised passage. No trial has been run.
reviewer.answer:
Response: We will separate the reported preference from the proposed consequence. The revision below gives the survey count and limits it to respondents. It also identifies attendance under extended hours as a question for a future trial. We have not run that trial and will not describe increased use as a result.

Revised passage: Eighteen of the thirty respondents requested evening access. This preference supports examining an evening opening option, but it does not show how many visitors would use it. A trial with attendance recorded by hour could address that question.
moves: The response addresses the substantive concern.
Planned empirical work is not claimed as completed.
The revised passage actually demonstrates the clarification.
reviewer.transfer: Supply both requested parts, and distinguish text you revise now from empirical work you only propose.
reviewer.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.

plain-revision.subject: A library
plain-revision.task: Revise: “Our revolutionary survey unlocks unparalleled access for everyone.” Facts: 18 of 30 respondents requested evening access; no schedule was changed. Explain two changes.
plain-revision.answer:
Revision: Eighteen of the thirty survey respondents requested evening access. Their responses identify a scheduling option for the library to examine. The survey does not show whether other visitors share that preference or whether longer opening would increase attendance. A trial could address actual use before a permanent change is made.

Change 1: I replaced a promotional claim with the count the survey supplies.
Change 2: I separated a request for access from evidence that a schedule change has delivered it.
moves: Concrete evidence replaces promotion.
Meaning is reconstructed from the brief rather than preserved when it is unsupported.
The two explanations tell the reader why the revision helps.
plain-revision.transfer: Replace inflated or unsupported claims with warranted ideas. Do not merely swap them for more formal synonyms.
plain-revision.provenance: Original constructed teaching example; not a research finding.
